item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q001_histone_related_proteins","answer":"In SCOPe, the canonical nucleosomal histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 are all-alpha proteins in the Histone-fold fold (a.22) and Histone-fold superfamily (a.22.1). Their close variants—such as H2A.Z, H2A.X, CENP-A, and H3.3—belong with their corresponding core-histone lineages at the family level, supporting relatively close homology but not identical biological roles. Archaeal histones, including HMf-like proteins, also have the histone fold and are homologous to eukaryotic core histones, although their simpler oligomers and chromatin organization do not justify transferring nucleosome-specific functions directly. More distant nonhistone members of the histone-fold superfamily include paired transcription-factor subunits such as TFIID TAFs, NF-YB/NF-YC, and NC2/Dr1–DRAP1; centromeric CENP-T/W/S/X proteins also contain histone-fold domains. These proteins share the characteristic three-helix histone-fold architecture and, when SCOPe places them in a.22.1, probable remote ancestry, but they occupy distinct families and their transcriptional or centromeric functions cannot be inferred from core histones. Fold-level similarity alone is weaker than family- or superfamily-level assignment and is insufficient for detailed function transfer or confident close-homology template selection. Conversely, proteins merely described as “histone-like,” notably bacterial HU/IHF, and linker histone H1 are not core-histone-fold homologs on that name alone and belong to different structural groupings. Exact domain membership and representative choice remain release- and construct-dependent; full-length multidomain proteins should be compared through the classified histone-fold domain rather than globally.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
